title: Arrangements with repeats
objectives: Count arrangements of letters when some letters repeat.
Explain why we divide by the factorial of each group of repeats.
Count grid routes and price paths as words with repeats.

screens.title: Arrangements with repeats
screens.prose: Some words repeat a letter, and some price paths repeat a move. Swapping two identical things changes nothing, so we must stop counting those swaps.
You have three letter cards: one E and two Gs. The two G cards look exactly alike.
screens.question: How many different three-letter strings can you make using all three cards?

hints.text: Where can the E go?
Once the E is placed, the two Gs fill the other places.
The E goes first, in the middle or last: EGG, GEG, GGE. Is there any other?

feedback.correct: Three strings: the E's place decides everything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place the E first, then fill the gaps with the Gs.

byKey.all-orders: You counted $3! = 6$ orders, as if the cards were all different. Swapping the two Gs gives the same string, so some of your orders repeat.
byKey.with-repeats: You let each place take any letter, $3 \times 3 \times 3$. You have only one E and two Gs to use.

explain.text: The E can sit in any of the 3 places, and the Gs fill the rest. That gives EGG, GEG and GGE. The Gs have no order of their own, so there are 3 strings, not $3! = 6$.

screens.prose: Paint a small 1 and 2 on the G cards so we can tell them apart. Now the cards differ, so there are $3! = 6$ orders. Tap a cell to select it, and tap it again to clear it.
screens.question: Tap every labelled order that reads GEG once the paint is rubbed off.

hints.text: Ignore the small numbers. Which orders have the E in the middle?
This one reads GEG. Its twin swaps the two labels.

feedback.correct: Two labelled orders read GEG: the Gs can carry their labels either way round.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rub off the small numbers in your head, and keep the orders with E in the middle.

byKey.r2c3: You found G₁ E G₂. Its twin G₂ E G₁ reads GEG too.
byKey.r1c1: You found G₂ E G₁. Its twin G₁ E G₂ reads GEG too.
byKey.r1c2: E G₁ G₂ reads EGG. The E has to be in the middle.
byKey.r2c1: E G₂ G₁ reads EGG. The E has to be in the middle.
byKey.r1c3: G₂ G₁ E reads GGE. The E has to be in the middle.
byKey.r2c2: G₁ G₂ E reads GGE. The E has to be in the middle.

explain.text: Each string appears twice: once with G₁ first and once with G₂ first. So the 6 labelled orders pair up into 3 strings, and $\tfrac{3!}{2} = 3$.

screens.prose: BOOK repeats the O. Label the Os $O_1$ and $O_2$, and the grid lists all $4! = 24$ labelled orders. Each pair of twins sits side by side. Counting the words this way is **dividing out the repeats**.
screens.question: How many different arrangements of the letters of BOOK are there?

hints.text: How many labelled orders spell the same word?
These two cells differ only by swapping $O_1$ and $O_2$.
Every word appears twice among the 24, so divide 24 by $2! = 2$.

feedback.correct: Each word appears twice among the 24 labelled orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many labelled orders give one word, then divide.

byKey.labelled: You counted the labelled orders. $O_1$ and $O_2$ look the same once the labels go, so each word is counted twice.
byKey.twice: You divided by 2 twice, once for each O. The two Os form one group, and a group of 2 has $2! = 2$ orders.

explain.text: The 24 labelled orders come in twin pairs that differ only by swapping $O_1$ and $O_2$. So there are $\tfrac{4!}{2!} = \tfrac{24}{2} = 12$ words.

canvas.caption: BKOO appears twice: the twins swap $O_1$ and $O_2$

screens.prose: ERROR has five letters, and R appears three times. Label them $R_1$, $R_2$ and $R_3$: now there are $5! = 120$ labelled orders.
screens.question: How many different arrangements of the letters of ERROR are there?

hints.text: In how many orders can $R_1$, $R_2$ and $R_3$ sit in their three places?
These three places hold the Rs. Shuffling them never changes the word.
Each word is counted $3! = 6$ times among the 120. Divide 120 by 6.

feedback.correct: Each word appears $3! = 6$ times among the labelled orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the orders of the three Rs among themselves, then divide 120 by that.

byKey.by-two: You divided by 2, as for a pair. Three Rs can be put in $3! = 6$ orders, not 2.
byKey.by-three: You divided by 3, the number of Rs. Three Rs have $3! = 6$ orders among themselves.
byKey.labelled: That is the count with labels on. Once the labels go, shuffling the Rs gives the same word.

explain.text: Within any one word, the three Rs can carry their labels in $3! = 6$ ways, all looking the same. So each word was counted 6 times: $\tfrac{5!}{3!} = \tfrac{120}{6} = 20$.

screens.prose: BANANA repeats two letters: A three times and N twice. With every copy labelled there are $6! = 720$ orders.
screens.question: How many different arrangements of the letters of BANANA are there?

hints.text: The As can be shuffled among themselves, and so can the Ns.
The As fill three places and the Ns fill two.
Each word is counted $3!$ times for the As, and each of those $2!$ times for the Ns. Divide 720 by $3! \times 2! = 12$.

feedback.correct: Shuffling the As and the Ns multiply, so each word appears 12 times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how many labelled orders give one word, using both repeated letters.

byKey.only-a: You divided out the As but not the Ns. Swapping the two Ns also leaves the word unchanged.
byKey.only-n: You divided out the Ns but not the As. Shuffling the three As also leaves the word unchanged.
byKey.added: You divided by $3! + 2! = 8$. Each A order goes with each N order, so the counts multiply: $3! \times 2! = 12$.
byKey.labelled: That is the count with every copy labelled. The repeats still need dividing out.

explain.text: For any one word, the As can carry their labels in $3!$ ways and the Ns in $2!$ ways. By the product rule each word is counted $3! \times 2! = 12$ times, so there are $\tfrac{6!}{3!\,2!} = \tfrac{720}{12} = 60$.

screens.prose: A route walks from Start to End, one cell right (R) or up (U) at a time. Every route uses 3 Rs and 2 Us, in some order. The shaded route is R U R R U.

state.caption: One route: R U R R U

screens.question: How many different routes go from Start to End?

hints.text: Write a route as a word of Rs and Us. Which words are allowed?
This route is the word RURRU. Every other route is another order of the same five letters.
Count the arrangements of RRRUU: $\tfrac{5!}{3!\,2!}$.

feedback.correct: A route is an arrangement of RRRUU, and there are 10 of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each route is a word of 3 Rs and 2 Us. Count those words.

byKey.all-orders: You counted $5! = 120$, as if all five steps were different. Two R steps are the same move, so swapping them gives the same route.
byKey.only-r: You divided out the Rs but not the Us. Swapping the two U steps also gives the same route.
byKey.cells: You counted the cells. A route is a whole path of five steps, not one cell.
byKey.added: You added 3 and 2. Count the orders of the five steps, then divide out the repeats.

explain.text: Each route is a word with 3 Rs and 2 Us, and each such word is a route. So the routes are the arrangements of RRRUU: $\tfrac{5!}{3!\,2!} = \tfrac{120}{12} = 10$.

screens.prose: A sign maker sells letter tiles: B, O, O and K. One O tile is blue and the other is orange. Every different-looking row of the four tiles is sold as its own design.

state.caption: The two O tiles are different colours

screens.question: How many different designs are there?

options.why: You divided by $2!$ for the repeated O. The Os are different colours, so swapping them gives a design that looks different.
You divided by 2 twice. Nothing here looks alike, so nothing should be divided out.
You doubled $4!$ for the two colours. The 24 orders already put each coloured tile in every place.

hints.text: If you swap the blue O and the orange O, does the row look the same?
These two tiles can be told apart.
All four tiles look different, so every one of the $4!$ orders is a different design.

feedback.correct: Four tiles that all look different give $4! = 24$ designs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether swapping the two O tiles changes how the row looks.

byKey.divided: You divided by $2!$ for the repeated O. The Os are different colours, so swapping them gives a new design. Divide only when swapped items look exactly alike.

explain.text: Swapping the blue O and the orange O changes the look, so no two of the 24 orders match. Divide only when swapped objects look exactly alike. So all $4! = 24$ orders are different designs.

screens.prose: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters: one M, four Is, four Ss and two Ps. We will count its arrangements the way you did for BANANA.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Label every copy, such as $I_1$ to $I_4$. All 11 letters now differ, so there are $11!$ labelled orders.
Fix one word. Its Is can carry their labels in $4!$ ways, its Ss in $4!$ and its Ps in $2!$.
By the product rule, each word appears $4!\,4!\,2!$ times among the labelled orders.
So the number of words is $\dfrac{11!}{4!\,4!\,2!} = 34\,650$.

hints.text: Start with the step that makes every letter different.
Before you can divide, you need to know how often each word is counted.
Label, count the relabellings of one word, multiply them, then divide.

feedback.correct: Each word is counted once for every relabelling of its repeats, so we divide by all of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count with labels first, then find how often each word was counted.

byKey.divide: The division needs the count from the line before it. Divide last.

explain.text: Labelling turns the problem into one you can solve: $11!$. Each word was then counted $4!\,4!\,2! = 1152$ times, so there are $\tfrac{39\,916\,800}{1152} = 34\,650$ words. In general, $n$ objects with groups of $k_1, k_2, \ldots$ identical copies have $\tfrac{n!}{k_1!\,k_2!\cdots}$ arrangements.

screens.prose: A stock closes up (U) or down (D) each day of a five-day week. It starts at £50.00 and moves £1.00 each day. Every week with exactly two down days ends at £51.00.

state.caption: One week with two down days: UUDUD

screens.question: How many weekly patterns have exactly two down days?

hints.text: A pattern is a word of five letters. Which letters, and how many of each?
Swapping the two Ds leaves the pattern the same, and so does shuffling the Us.
Count the arrangements of UUUDD: $\tfrac{5!}{3!\,2!}$.

feedback.correct: A pattern is an arrangement of UUUDD: 10 of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write a pattern as a word of 3 Us and 2 Ds, then count the arrangements.

byKey.only-u: You divided out the three Us but not the two Ds. Swapping the down days also gives the same pattern.
byKey.all-orders: You counted $5!$, as if every day's move were a different letter. The repeats need dividing out.
byKey.all-weeks: That is every pattern, $2^5$. Only those with exactly two Ds count.

explain.text: A pattern is an arrangement of UUUDD, so there are $\tfrac{5!}{3!\,2!} = 10$. It is also a choice of which 2 of the 5 days are down: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$. Price paths in a tree are counted the same way.

ideas: Label the repeated copies, count all the labelled orders, then divide by the ways to relabel each group.
Groups relabel independently, so divide by the product $k_1!\,k_2!\cdots$. A letter that appears once divides by $1! = 1$.
A grid route of Rs and Us, or a price path of ups and downs, is a word with repeats.

formula.name: Arrangements with repeats
formula.note: $n$ objects in all: $k_1$ alike of one kind, $k_2$ alike of another, and so on.

summary.trap: Divide only when swapped objects look exactly alike. Two tiles of different colours are different objects.

quiz.prose: The word LEVEL has five letters: two Ls, two Es and one V.
quiz.question: How many different arrangements of its letters are there?

options.why: You divided out one repeated letter only. Both the Ls and the Es repeat.
You divided by $2!$ for the V as well. V appears once, and $1! = 1$.
You counted $5!$, as if all five letters were different.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $5!$ by the orders of each repeated letter.

explain.text: The Ls relabel in $2!$ ways and the Es in $2!$ ways, and the V in $1! = 1$. So there are $\tfrac{120}{2 \times 2} = 30$ arrangements.

quiz.prose: Four identical £1.00 coins are laid in a row.
quiz.question: How many different-looking rows are there?

feedback.correct: Every order looks the same: just one row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap any two coins. Does the row change?

byKey.all-orders: You counted $4!$ orders. The coins are identical, so every order looks the same.
byKey.by-four: You divided by 4. The four coins can be shuffled in $4! = 24$ ways.

explain.text: All four coins are one group of identical copies, so we divide $4!$ by $4!$. That leaves $1$: the edge case where everything repeats.

quiz.prose: On a larger grid, every route from Start to End takes 4 steps right and 3 steps up.
quiz.question: How many routes are there?

feedback.correct: The routes are the arrangements of RRRRUUU.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each route as a word of 4 Rs and 3 Us.

byKey.all-orders: You counted $7!$, as if all seven steps differed. Steps in the same direction are alike.
byKey.only-r: You divided out the Rs but not the Us.
byKey.added: You added the steps. Count the orders of the seven steps, then divide out the repeats.

explain.text: Each route is an arrangement of 4 Rs and 3 Us. So there are $\tfrac{7!}{4!\,3!} = \tfrac{5040}{144} = 35$ routes.

quiz.prose: A price moves up or down at each of 6 steps.
quiz.question: How many price paths have exactly 4 up moves?

options.why: You divided out the four ups but not the two downs.
That is every path, $2^6$. Only those with exactly 4 ups count.
You counted $\tfrac{6!}{2!}$, dividing out the downs only. The ups are alike too.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A path is a word of 4 Us and 2 Ds.

explain.text: A path with 4 ups is an arrangement of UUUUDD. There are $\tfrac{720}{24 \times 2} = 15$ of them.
